1.title: Relative Motion on a Bus
1.text:
Relative Motion on a Bus

The speed you measure for an object depends on the coordinate system you measure it from.

Our big question for this lesson: does how you describe motion depend on your frame of reference? Picture yourself on a school bus moving at 8 meters per second in the positive direction. You walk toward the front of the bus at 1 meter per second. A friend standing beside the road watches the bus go by. How fast does your friend say you're moving?

Your friend, in a coordinate system fixed to the road, measures the bus at 8 meters per second. If you stand still on the bus, your speed relative to the road is also 8 meters per second, but your speed relative to the bus is zero. How can you have two different speeds at once?

testIt.name: Relative Motion on a Bus
testIt.how: Ride a bus and switch between the bus view and the roadside view to see your own speed change.

2.title: Reference Frames
2.text:
Reference Frames

A reference frame is a coordinate system from which motion is viewed.

Here, your motion is viewed from different coordinate systems. A coordinate system from which motion is viewed is called a reference frame. Walking at 1 meter per second toward the front of the bus is your velocity in the bus's reference frame. In the road's reference frame, your velocity is different.

So restate the problem: given the bus's velocity relative to the road and your velocity relative to the bus, what's your velocity relative to the road? Figure 13 shows this with vectors. The length of each velocity vector shows its speed. If right is positive, your speed relative to the road is 9 meters per second, the sum of 8 meters per second and 1 meter per second.

Now walk at the same speed toward the back of the bus. Figure 13 shows that because the two velocities point in opposite directions, your speed relative to the road is 7 meters per second, the difference between 8 and 1. When velocities lie along the same line, simple addition or subtraction gives the relative velocity. You add when they point the same way, and subtract when they point opposite ways.

testIt.name: Reference Frames
testIt.how: Set the bus speed and your walking speed and direction and see the roadside speed as a sum or difference of the two arrows.

3.title: Your Investigation Toolkit
3.text:
Your Investigation Toolkit

Use your Science Journal to record the evidence you collect during this lesson's readings and activities. As you read, build a table of crosscutting concepts and fill in examples as you find them.

Online, the PhysicsLAB called Moving Reference Frame has you carry out an investigation of how a system's motion looks in different reference frames.

4.title: Combining Velocity Vectors
4.text:
Combining Velocity Vectors

The velocity of a relative to c is the vector sum of a's velocity relative to b and b's velocity relative to c: v sub a over b plus v sub b over c equals v sub a over c.

Let's look closer at how we got the velocities in Figure 13. Is there a rule for combining velocities in a moving reference frame? Call the bus's velocity relative to the road v sub b over r. Call your velocity relative to the bus v sub y over b, and your velocity relative to the road v sub y over r.

In both cases, you found your velocity relative to the road by adding your velocity relative to the bus and the bus's velocity relative to the road. Mathematically, v sub y over b plus v sub b over r equals v sub y over r.

The more general form is the relative velocity equation. The velocity of object a relative to object c is the vector sum of a's velocity relative to b and b's velocity relative to c: v sub a over b plus v sub b over c equals v sub a over c. For example, a flea running on the back of a dog that's running along a road has a velocity relative to the road of v sub flea over dog plus v sub dog over road.

testIt.name: Combining Velocity Vectors
testIt.how: A flea on a dog on a road: you set each velocity and watch the subscripts chain together into the flea's velocity relative to the road.

5.title: STEM Career Connection, Commercial Pilot
5.text:
STEM Career Connection, Commercial Pilot

Pilots use relative motion and projectile motion to reach their destinations and targets.

Want to be a commercial pilot? You'll need to understand relative motion to get a plane or helicopter to its destination. And pilots who drop fire-retardant gel to fight forest fires also need to understand projectile motion to hit their targets.

6.title: Relative Motion in Two Dimensions
6.text:
Relative Motion in Two Dimensions

In two dimensions, place velocity vectors tip to tail; the resultant is the velocity relative to the ground reference frame.

Adding relative velocities works in two dimensions too. As in one dimension, first draw a vector diagram, then solve the problem with math.

Figure 14 shows how to draw these diagrams. The velocity vectors go tip to tail. The reference frame you're viewing from, often called the ground reference frame, is treated as being at rest. One vector gives the velocity of the second reference frame relative to the ground. The other vector gives the motion within that moving frame. The resultant is the relative velocity, the velocity relative to the ground reference frame. In the subscripts, o over g means the object relative to the ground, o over m means the object relative to the moving frame, and m over g means the moving frame relative to the ground.

And yes, anything moving can serve as a reference frame, including a moving car.

testIt.name: Relative Motion in Two Dimensions
testIt.how: Drag a moving-frame vector and an object-in-frame vector tip to tail and watch the ground-frame resultant form.

7.title: Airplanes and Boats
7.text:
Airplanes and Boats

A plane's velocity relative to the ground is the sum of its velocity relative to the air and the wind's velocity relative to the ground.

Airplanes are a great example. Airline pilots can't just aim along a compass direction and expect to arrive. They have to account for the plane's speed relative to the air, shown by the airspeed indicator, and its direction relative to the air. They also have to consider the wind's velocity relative to the ground at their altitude.

Those two vectors combine to give the plane's velocity relative to the ground. The resultant tells the pilot how fast, and in what direction, the plane will travel relative to the ground to reach its destination.

Boats on flowing water face the same situation. A boat can even stay in one place relative to the shore by heading upstream with a speed relative to the water equal to the speed of the current. The two velocities cancel.

testIt.name: Airplanes and Boats
testIt.how: Fly a plane with an adjustable wind and steer to reach a target airport, then hold a boat still against a river current.

8.title: Combining Velocities with Components
8.text:
Combining Velocities with Components

v sub o over m plus v sub m over g equals v sub o over g; resolve each into x- and y-components to find the magnitude.

You can use the equations in Figure 15 to solve two-dimensional relative motion problems. The velocity of a reference frame moving relative to the ground is v sub m over g. The velocity of an object in the moving frame is v sub o over m. The relative velocity equation gives the object's velocity relative to the ground: v sub o over m plus v sub m over g equals v sub o over g.

To find the size of the object's velocity relative to the ground, first resolve the velocity of the object and the velocity of the moving frame into x- and y-components. Then apply the Pythagorean theorem. Figure 15 shows the general equation, but many problems are simpler, because the vectors lie along an axis. And as the next example shows, you can find the angle of the object's velocity relative to the ground by looking at the vector diagram and using a trigonometric relationship.

So vectors describe relative motion in two dimensions by placing the frame's velocity and the object's velocity tip to tail and adding them, component by component.

testIt.name: Combining Velocities with Components
testIt.how: Set a moving frame's velocity and an object's velocity at any angles and see the x and y components add into the ground-frame velocity.

9.title: Example Problem 4, Relative Velocity of a Marble
9.text:
Example Problem 4, Relative Velocity of a Marble

For perpendicular velocities, use the Pythagorean theorem for the speed and the inverse tangent for the direction.

Ana and Sandra are riding a ferry boat heading east at 4.0 meters per second. Sandra rolls a marble north, straight across the deck to Ana, at 0.75 meters per second. What's the marble's velocity relative to the water?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Set up a coordinate system and draw vectors for the velocities. Known: the boat's velocity relative to the water is 4.0 meters per second, and the marble's velocity relative to the boat is 0.75 meters per second. Unknown: the marble's velocity relative to the water.

Step two: solve. The velocities are perpendicular, so use the Pythagorean theorem. The marble's speed relative to the water squared equals the boat's velocity squared plus the marble's velocity relative to the boat squared. Take the square root: the square root of the square of 4.0 meters per second plus the square of 0.75 meters per second, which is 4.1 meters per second. For the angle, theta equals the inverse tangent of 0.75 meters per second over 4.0 meters per second, which is 11 degrees north of east. So the marble travels at 4.1 meters per second, 11 degrees north of east.

Step three: evaluate. Dimensional analysis confirms meters per second for velocity. The signs should all be positive, and they are. And the result is the same order of magnitude as the given velocities, just a bit bigger than the larger one.

testIt.name: Example Problem 4
testIt.how: Roll a marble across a moving ferry and toggle between the deck view and the water view to see its straight and slanted paths.

10.title: STEM at Work, Fighting Fire with Forces
10.text:
STEM at Work, Fighting Fire with Forces

Smokejumpers are professional wildland firefighters who parachute into remote areas to fight wildfires.

Smokejumpers are professional wildland firefighters who parachute into remote areas to control and put out wildfires. It's an incredibly dangerous job. They jump from planes at least 450 meters above the ground, and with today's steerable parachutes at least 900 meters, into areas near blazing fires. How do they land safely? It takes extensive training and an understanding of two-dimensional motion.

Firefighters accepted into a smokejumper program already have extensive experience fighting wildland fires. Even so, they go through rigorous training. They learn to exit an airplane properly, open their parachutes, and land safely. They also get first aid training and practice climbing trees and digging fire lines.

When smokejumpers leave the plane, they move in two dimensions at once, along both the x- and y-axes. The initial push that launches them and the force of gravity both act on them, and gravity curves their path downward, roughly a projectile path. They have to plan their trajectories so they land somewhere safe. A spotter flies on every mission, accounting for wind speed and direction to help plan the paths of both the jumpers and their supply packages. Those packages hold firefighting tools, food, and water, so smokejumpers can work on their own for the first 48 hours. Spotters also report how and where the fire is moving.

On the ground, smokejumpers dig fire lines to contain fires. They set backfires, which burn toward the main fire to remove fuel in its path. From above, aircraft drop water and fire retardant. Together, these crews protect huge stretches of wildland every year. Now your turn: write a problem about a smokejumper's trajectory, swap with a classmate, and solve each other's problems.

testIt.name: STEM at Work
testIt.how: Set a plane's speed, release height, and wind and drop a supply package, trying to land it in a safe zone.
